# Migrate the landscape view to Dioxus (static SSR + feature-gated live/multiplayer mode)

## Context

`src/view/html.rs` builds the `residual view`/`residual serve` landscape page by hand: string
concatenation and `.replace()` on placeholders in `src/view/template.html`. This already needed a
large rewrite for the matrix-viewport-blind fix (just committed as `25a24a7`), and the next planned
step — a "multiplayer" mode where several browsers watch and edit the same landscape live, with a
single operator resolving any conflicts — is more restructuring than the string-templating approach
can reasonably absorb. Dioxus was chosen because one component tree can render two ways: `dioxus-ssr`
to a static `String` (today's `view`/`serve`, no async runtime needed), and `dioxus-liveview`
(server-authoritative, pushes DOM diffs over a websocket) for the live mode later. The static build
must never contain live-mode code — enforced via a Cargo feature flag, not a runtime check.

Two exploration passes confirmed the groundwork:
- **View layer**: `render_landscape_html` (`src/view/html.rs:26`) is called from `write_landscape_html`
  and `build_serve_document` in `src/view/mod.rs`; `run_serve` renders once at startup and hands the
  same bytes to every `tiny_http` request (no polling). The client JS in `template.html` has no
  fetch/WebSocket anywhere today — a load-bearing test,
  `html_command_generator_does_not_mutate_the_ledger`, asserts exactly that. `src/view/commands.rs`
  already has `StagedAdd`/`format_add_command`/`shell_quote` — a server-side, JSON-serializable model
  of a staged `residual add …` command, built so its variants mirror `crate::cli::AddTarget` — this is
  the natural pending-additions shape for live mode, no need to invent a new one.
- **Storage layer**: `src/storage/write_authorization.rs` (`authorize(cfg, minutes)` /
  `require(cfg)`) is an explicitly short-lived (default 30 min), single-operator model — comment says
  so directly. `integrity::sessions` uses a 30s advisory lock, silently stolen when stale. Every
  mutation (`src/storage/stressors.rs` etc.) does a full CSV read-rewrite, and `git_sidecar.rs` commits
  synchronously per mutation. None of this tolerates a long-running process doing per-keystroke writes
  — confirmed by direct exploration, not assumption.

Given that, the user decided: Dioxus; static build has zero live code (feature flag); live mode allows
concurrent edits with the operator resolving conflicts manually (no CRDT — "netcode" is future work);
live mode holds an **in-memory authoritative snapshot**, mutated directly and broadcast instantly, with
disk persistence only via an explicit, idempotent **Save** button that retries once through an
auto-reauthorize flow if `write_authorization::require` rejects it; and the existing copy-paste
command-generator surface is kept *alongside* Save, both reading the same staged-additions state.

This plan covers milestone (a) only in full implementation detail — the static-path refactor, which is
safe, mechanical, and independently mergeable — and lays out the follow-on live-mode milestones at the
level needed to sequence them, without writing live-mode code yet (it depends on Dioxus/dioxus-liveview
API specifics that need verifying against current docs first).

## Approach

Keep `render_landscape_html`/`extract_snapshot_json` as the stable public contract re-exported from
`src/view/mod.rs` (`pub use html::render_landscape_html` → `pub use static_export::render_landscape_html`),
so `write_landscape_html`/`build_serve_document`/`run_view`/`run_serve` need no changes at all. Move the
16 string-building functions in `src/view/html.rs` into Dioxus components under `src/view/components/`,
render them via `dioxus-ssr`, and splice the resulting fragments into the **same** `template.html` shell
(renamed `src/view/shell.html`) at the same placeholders it uses today. The CSS and client JS
(filter/sort/accordion/threshold-slider/command-generator) stay untouched, unmoved static text — they're
pure DOM-local behavior that doesn't care whether the surrounding HTML came from `.replace()` or
`dioxus-ssr`, and rewriting them as Dioxus signals would put five existing tests
(`template_wires_*`) at risk for zero behavioral gain.

### Files

- **`Cargo.toml`**: add `dioxus` and `dioxus-ssr` as always-on dependencies (no `[features]` yet — that
  arrives with live mode). Before pinning exact versions, verify against current docs: whether
  `dioxus-ssr` needs the full `dioxus` crate/macro feature or just `dioxus-core`, and confirm the
  current SSR entrypoint name (`dioxus_ssr::render(&VirtualDom)` or similar) — do not guess semver or
  API shape from training data, since Dioxus's SSR API has moved between versions.
- **`src/view/components/`** (new): `mod.rs`, `matrix.rs`, `defense.rs`. Map of old → new:
  - `render_matrix` + header/row/totals loops → `matrix.rs`: `MatrixTable`, `ForceRow`,
    `MatrixTotalsRow` components, props built from `&LandscapeSnapshot` slices (clone into owned props
    if Dioxus's current prop model doesn't ergonomically support the borrows `html.rs` uses today —
    snapshots are small, cloning is cheap here).
  - `force_label`, `force_kind_attr`, `status_bucket`, `status_tooltip`, `row_total`, `col_total`,
    `architecture_sets_for_force` → stay as plain functions in `matrix.rs`, called from components
    (pure computation, no reason to become components themselves).
  - `render_defense_records`, `render_meta_force_item`, `render_meta_attractor_item`,
    `render_defense_forms` → `defense.rs`: `DefenseRecords`, `MetaForceItem`, `MetaAttractorItem`,
    `DefenseForms` components, props from `&DefenseSection`/`&SnapshotMetaForce`/`&SnapshotAttractor`.
  - `esc` → likely deleted for text nodes (Dioxus escapes text automatically); keep a small
    `esc_attr` helper in `matrix.rs` for hand-formatted attribute strings (e.g. `data-search`) that
    Dioxus's automatic escaping doesn't cover.
  - **Hard constraint**: rendered tag names, attribute names, and attribute value formatting (e.g.
    `data-force-id="S-01"`, boolean `hidden`) must byte-match what the existing tests assert — Dioxus's
    SSR serialization of booleans/self-closing tags can differ from hand-built HTML, so this needs
    checking early, not assumed.
- **`src/view/static_export.rs`** (new, replaces `src/view/html.rs`): `render_landscape_html`,
  `extract_snapshot_json`, `escape_script_json`, `SNAPSHOT_PLACEHOLDER`/`SNAPSHOT_ELEMENT_ID` move here
  unchanged; the matrix/defense-forms/defense-records placeholders are now filled by
  `dioxus_ssr::render(...)` output of the new components instead of hand-built strings.
- **`src/view/shell.html`** (renamed from `template.html`): content unchanged.
- **`src/view/mod.rs`**: change one `pub use` line (`html::render_landscape_html` →
  `static_export::render_landscape_html`) and the module declaration (`pub mod html;` →
  `pub mod static_export;`). Nothing else in this file changes — its own tests
  (`view_writes_html_to_temp_dir_and_prints_path`, `serve_document_matches_the_view_html_for_the_same_config`,
  etc., `src/view/mod.rs:319-554`) already only assert through the public API and stay green untouched.
- **Delete** `src/view/html.rs` and the old `src/view/template.html` once parity is confirmed.

### Test migration (colocated, per this repo's convention)

All ~19 tests currently in `src/view/html.rs` (`html_embeds_snapshot_json_in_a_script_block`,
`html_matrix_rows_carry_filterable_force_data`, `html_force_rows_are_accordions_labeled_by_shortname`,
`html_matrix_has_row_and_column_totals`, `html_matrix_carries_sticky_hooks`,
`html_matrix_headers_carry_sort_and_status_metadata`, `html_filter_js_and_rendered_rows_share_the_same_data_hooks`,
`html_contains_residue_matrix_with_cell_data_attributes`, `html_contains_command_generator_and_copy_surface`,
`html_command_generator_does_not_mutate_the_ledger`, `html_omits_defense_forms_and_records_without_defense`,
`html_includes_defense_forms_and_records_with_defense`, `html_escapes_script_terminator_in_snapshot_values`,
plus the five `template_wires_*`/`template_asset_carries_placeholder_and_generator_js` tests) move to
`src/view/static_export.rs`'s `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`, calling the same public functions with the same
assertions — the `template_wires_*` ones just rename the constant they assert against (`TEMPLATE` →
`SHELL`). **`html_command_generator_does_not_mutate_the_ledger` is the one that matters most**: it must
keep passing unchanged, since it's the direct evidence that the static path never gains a
fetch/XHR/sendBeacon call as a side effect of this refactor.

Add one **temporary** test during the migration —
`static_export_matches_legacy_html_byte_for_byte` — rendering both the old `html.rs` path and the new
component path against the same fixture snapshot (`src/view/mod.rs`'s `testing::fixture_main_snapshot`/
`fixture_defense_snapshot` are already built for exactly this) and asserting byte-equality. Delete it
once parity is confirmed and `html.rs` is removed — it's a migration aid, not a permanent contract.

### Verification

1. `cargo test` — full suite green, in particular every test named above plus
   `src/view/mod.rs`'s existing view/serve tests.
2. `cargo build` (no new features) — confirm via `cargo tree` that only `dioxus`/`dioxus-ssr` were
   added, nothing async/web-framework-shaped leaked in transitively.
3. Manual smoke check: `nix develop -c residual view` and open the printed path in a browser (or
   `nix develop -c residual serve` and hit `127.0.0.1:8787`) — confirm the matrix, accordions, filter,
   sort, and command-generator copy surface all still work exactly as before. This is cheap insurance
   against SSR attribute-serialization drift that a passing test suite might not catch if a test's
   substring assertion happens to survive a subtly wrong rendering.
4. `nix develop -c residual verify all` before committing (per project convention), and commit only
   the view-layer files, following the `<component>: S-<nn>: summary` commit-message convention enforced
   by this repo's `commit-msg` hook (this work is a continuation of `matrix-viewport-blind`/S-26 and
   `residue-matrix-shape`/S-27).

## Follow-on: live/multiplayer mode (sequenced, not detailed yet)

These come after the static migration lands and are gated behind a new `live` Cargo feature
(`axum`, `tokio`, `dioxus-liveview` as `optional = true`, pulled in only by `live = ["dep:axum", "dep:tokio", "dep:dioxus-liveview"]`),
with the entire `src/view/live/` module behind `#[cfg(feature = "live")]` so a plain `cargo build`
never parses, let alone links, any of it:

- **(b) Liveview skeleton**: `src/view/live/{mod.rs,server.rs,liveview.rs}` — axum server +
  dioxus-liveview wired to render one `LandscapePage` component (same components from milestone (a))
  over a websocket. No shared/mutable state yet — just prove the plumbing. New
  `#[cfg(feature = "live")]`-gated `Command::Live` in `src/cli.rs`. **Before writing this**, verify
  current `dioxus-liveview`'s supported axum/tokio version pairing and its axum-integration entrypoint
  against current docs — this pairing is historically narrow and shouldn't be guessed.
- **(c) In-memory `LiveState`**: `src/view/live/state.rs` — `LiveState { snapshot: LandscapeSnapshot, pending: Vec<StagedAdd> }`
  behind a lock, broadcasting re-renders to connected clients on change. Prove broadcast independent of
  mutation first (e.g. a debug-triggered reload).
  **This is the piece that quietly walks back the doc comment at the top of `src/view/commands.rs`**
  ("The landscape UI never mutates the ledger") for the live path specifically — worth a short doc
  update there noting the static path keeps that invariant, live mode intentionally doesn't.
- **(d) Browser-originated mutations**: staging-form submissions append a `StagedAdd` to
  `LiveState.pending` and broadcast to all clients — this is where "concurrent edits visible to
  everyone, operator resolves conflicts" actually lands, and it's deliberately just list-append, no
  merge logic.
- **(e) Save button**: `src/view/live/save.rs`, `flush_pending(cfg, state)`:
  1. Empty `pending` → `Ok(())` immediately (idempotency).
  2. Convert each `StagedAdd` to `crate::cli::AddTarget` (new `StagedAdd::into_add_target`, colocated
     in `src/view/commands.rs` since the variants already mirror `AddTarget` 1:1) and call
     `crate::storage::add(cfg, target, force)` for each.
  3. On a `write_authorization`-shaped failure, call
     `crate::storage::write_authorization::authorize(cfg, write_authorization::DEFAULT_MINUTES)` once
     and retry the batch — the try→fail→reauth→try flow requested.
  4. On success, clear `pending` and broadcast, so a second Save with nothing new is a true no-op.
  5. Note for the user up front: this reuses `storage::add` as-is per instruction, so each pending item
     is still a full CSV rewrite + a git-sidecar commit if enabled — a large batch takes a few seconds,
     not milliseconds.
- **(f) Command-generator panel in live mode**: `commands_panel.rs` renders
  `format_add_commands(&state.pending)` (already exists, reused verbatim) server-side, so Save and the
  copy-paste surface read the same `LiveState.pending` — satisfying "both are useful, both see the same
  staged list."

Each of (b)–(f) should land as its own reviewable, independently-tested change.

# Migrate the landscape view to Dioxus (static SSR + feature-gated live/multiplayer mode)

## Context

`src/view/html.rs` builds the `residual view`/`residual serve` landscape page by hand: string
concatenation and `.replace()` on placeholders in `src/view/template.html`. This already needed a
large rewrite for the matrix-viewport-blind fix (just committed as `25a24a7`), and the next planned
step — a "multiplayer" mode where several browsers watch and edit the same landscape live, with a
single operator resolving any conflicts — is more restructuring than the string-templating approach
can reasonably absorb. Dioxus was chosen because one component tree can render two ways: `dioxus-ssr`
to a static `String` (today's `view`/`serve`, no async runtime needed), and `dioxus-liveview`
(server-authoritative, pushes DOM diffs over a websocket) for the live mode later. The static build
must never contain live-mode code — enforced via a Cargo feature flag, not a runtime check.

Two exploration passes confirmed the groundwork:
- **View layer**: `render_landscape_html` (`src/view/html.rs:26`) is called from `write_landscape_html`
  and `build_serve_document` in `src/view/mod.rs`; `run_serve` renders once at startup and hands the
  same bytes to every `tiny_http` request (no polling). The client JS in `template.html` has no
  fetch/WebSocket anywhere today — a load-bearing test,
  `html_command_generator_does_not_mutate_the_ledger`, asserts exactly that. `src/view/commands.rs`
  already has `StagedAdd`/`format_add_command`/`shell_quote` — a server-side, JSON-serializable model
  of a staged `residual add …` command, built so its variants mirror `crate::cli::AddTarget` — this is
  the natural pending-additions shape for live mode, no need to invent a new one.
- **Storage layer**: `src/storage/write_authorization.rs` (`authorize(cfg, minutes)` /
  `require(cfg)`) is an explicitly short-lived (default 30 min), single-operator model — comment says
  so directly. `integrity::sessions` uses a 30s advisory lock, silently stolen when stale. Every
  mutation (`src/storage/stressors.rs` etc.) does a full CSV read-rewrite, and `git_sidecar.rs` commits
  synchronously per mutation. None of this tolerates a long-running process doing per-keystroke writes
  — confirmed by direct exploration, not assumption.

Given that, the user decided: Dioxus; static build has zero live code (feature flag); live mode allows
concurrent edits with the operator resolving conflicts manually (no CRDT — "netcode" is future work);
live mode holds an **in-memory authoritative snapshot**, mutated directly and broadcast instantly, with
disk persistence only via an explicit, idempotent **Save** button that retries once through an
auto-reauthorize flow if `write_authorization::require` rejects it; and the existing copy-paste
command-generator surface is kept *alongside* Save, both reading the same staged-additions state.

safe, mechanical, and independently mergeable — and lays out the follow-on live-mode milestones at the
level needed to sequence them, without writing live-mode code yet (it depends on Dioxus/dioxus-liveview
API specifics that need verifying against current docs first).

(`template_wires_*`) at risk for zero behavioral gain.

  arrives with live mode). Before pinning exact versions, verify against current docs: whether

`html_command_generator_does_not_mutate_the_ledger`, `html_omits_defense_forms_and_records_without_defense`,

Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

name: tdd-implement
version: 0
description: >-
  Commit first, then orchestrate R/G TDD with subagents: first subagent writes all
  failing (red) tests, parent verifies, subsequent subagents implement phase-by-phase
  with prior-phase context, parent verifies between phases and passes pointers, final
  verification before handoff. Use when implementing features, refactors, or bug fixes
  with tests; when the user says r/g-tdd, red/green TDD, rg-implement, or multi-phase
  implementation with subagents.
---

# tdd-implement

Commit first. r/g-tdd with subagents — the first subagent makes all red, you verify, the 2..nth use r/g-tdd per phase and receive context about what the prior agents have done in order to keep on track, you verify between each phase and pass pointers as you see fit to subagents, then you do one final verification at the end before handoff.

## Workflow

```
Progress:
- [ ] 0. Commit first (baseline before any test or implementation work)
- [ ] 1. Subagent 1 — all red tests
- [ ] 2. Parent verify — tests fail for the right reasons
- [ ] 3. Subagent 2..n — R/G TDD per phase (with prior-phase context)
- [ ] 4. Parent verify between each phase; pass pointers to next subagent
- [ ] 5. Final verification before handoff
```

### 0. Commit first

Before spawning subagents or writing tests, commit the current working state so red
tests and implementation land on a clean baseline.

### 1. Subagent 1 — all red

Launch one subagent whose **only** job is to write failing tests for the full scope.
No implementation. Tests must fail for the intended missing behavior, not import/syntax errors.

### 2. Parent verify (red gate)

Run the test suite. Confirm:
- Tests fail (red)
- Failures match the intended contract gaps
- No spurious greens or broken harness

Only then proceed to implementation phases.

### 3. Subagent 2..n — R/G per phase

For each implementation phase:
1. Launch a subagent with **context from prior phases** (what was done, what remains, file pointers)
2. Subagent follows R/G TDD for **that phase only**: minimal code to go green, no scope creep
3. Parent verifies between phases before launching the next

### 4. Passing pointers

Between phases, give the next subagent:
- Summary of completed work
- Relevant file paths and function names
- Remaining phases / open failures
- Constraints or decisions made in earlier phases

### 5. Final verification

Before handoff:
- Full test suite green
- No unrelated regressions
- Scope matches original request
- Lints clean on touched files

## Subagent launch template

```
Task: Phase N of tdd-implement for [feature/bug].

Prior context:
- [what subagents 1..N-1 did]
- Files: [paths]
- Decisions: [constraints]

This phase:
- [specific R/G scope]
- Run: [test command]
- Stop when: [phase pass criteria]
```

## Anti-patterns

- Skipping commit-first — red tests mixed with unrelated WIP
- Subagent 1 implementing code — defeats the all-red gate
- Launching phase N without parent verify on phase N-1
- Passing subagents the full chat instead of distilled pointers
- Declaring done without final full-suite verification

| S-23 | software-only-zag | Operator prematurely decides on a software fix for a stressor and never examines hardware, process, organization, or policy zig | A-07 |
| S-24 | ceremony-lockout | Operator workflows are not considered — the tool demands a rigid full skill sequence and rejects a-la-carte use, so operators abandon residuality or fake compliance | A-06 |
| S-25 | attractor-valence-blind | Operator cannot tell why a stressor hurts the project because attractors lack paired positive and negative pressure — the stressor has nowhere coherent to land | A-09 |
| S-26 | matrix-viewport-blind | The NKP matrix is hard to read at dogfood scale — coupling heat does not read as a heatmap, row/column totals are missing or easy to lose, and headers/row labels scroll off-screen — so operators miss hyperliminal bands, fission candidates, and which forces drive K | A-06 |
| S-27 | residue-matrix-shape | residues.csv is already matrix-shaped (force × component cells), but at real project scale neither the CLI table nor raw CSV remains usable for filtering, zoom, multi-view exploration, or coherent landscape recall — spreadsheet-friendly shape alone does not yield operator fluency | A-19 |
| S-28 | lexicon-commit-drift | Operators use conventional commit prefixes (fix:/chore:/refactor:) that carry no project vocabulary — git log drifts from lexicon and components.csv | A-02 |
| S-29 | cli-bypass | Agent or operator edits residual/ CSVs directly (Python scripts, raw text edits, sed) for operations the residual CLI already supports — bypassing ID generation, idempotency guards, and verify | A-08 |
| S-30 | persona-context-pollution | When persona voices are generated inline alongside the main conversation they read the same context, share the same mental model, and produce shallow concerns that mirror what the operator already thinks — producing no new information and failing to surface real stressor pressure from external viewpoints | A-05 |
| S-31 | attractor-mission-conflation | An agent prompted to bootstrap an uninitialized ledger conflates an attractor with the system mission statement — bundling multiple concerns and omitting the negative state — producing a ledger that appears populated but carries no bifurcation signal for stressors to push against | A-09 |
| S-32 | force-component-drift | A stressor fires but the components listed on it did not need to change — the force-component mapping was anticipated incorrectly. Over time these mismatches accumulate unchecked: the matrix coupling analysis drifts from empirical reality, and no record exists to identify or correct the pattern | A-05 |
| S-33 | legacy-naive-change-ambiguity | At time of use, the agent encounters existing records and examples that use naive_change for assumptions, untreated behavior, and mechanistic adjustments interchangeably. | A-11 |
| S-34 | component-framed-input | At time of use, an actor supplies an incident or requirement narrative framed entirely through known components, concealing whether any force originates beyond the architecture iteration ergodic boundary. | A-09 |
| S-35 | authority-constrained-residue | At time of use, an actor identifies a whole-system adjustment that answers a stressor, but authority, ownership, budget, culture, or timing places that adjustment outside current control. | A-07 |
| S-36 | adverse-outcome-convention | At time of use, an actor brings a risk-analysis convention in which outcome means the adverse consequence of a stressor into residual force capture. | A-12 |
| S-37 | analytics-majority-collapse-tooling | A varied audience produces distinct operating contexts and event sequences, but actor-controlled analytics combine them into aggregate measurements that conceal state transitions. | A-13 |
| S-38 | analytics-majority-collapse-guidance | A varied audience produces distinct operating contexts and event sequences, but externally controlled analytics expose only aggregate measurements and the actor cannot alter their collection or presentation. | A-13 |
| S-39 | frequency-admission-tooling | Actor-controlled analytics rank observations by frequency and suppress less common coherent event sequences. | A-13 |
| S-40 | frequency-admission-guidance | Organizational or third-party analytics expose frequency-ranked observations while preventing the actor from changing collection, ranking, or retention. | A-13 |
| S-41 | id-centric-dialogue | As the ledger grows, precise agent session memory favors IDs while operator longitudinal memory retains names and concepts, causing ID-only references to break conversational continuity. | A-14 |
| S-42 | environmental-order-drift | Laws, handbooks, contracts, or established practices change after research is captured, while an actor later consults the superseded material during a walk. | A-13 |
| S-43 | documented-order-restriction | Authoritative research describes nominal behavior while exceptions and undocumented practices shape the environment, causing documented order to appear exhaustive. | A-13 |
| S-44 | research-context-pollution | An actor requests a broad research review whose volume, conflicts, or irrelevant detail displaces the active force and attractor context from the agent working context. | A-14 |
| S-45 | hyperliminal-model-reification | Repeated patterns in research appear stable enough that an actor treats them as a complete predictive model of the hyperliminal and dismisses contradictory configurations as noise. | A-13 |
| S-46 | landscape-review-decay | Project work proceeds without a regular cadence of architecture walks. As real-world force configurations evolve between reviews, recorded stressors and attractors remain static and the residual-architecture loses correspondence with its environment. | A-13 |
| S-47 | llm-degradation | An operator invokes a skill with whatever model is available to them — frontier, mid-tier, local, or open-weight — and that model's capability falls short of the skill's cognitive demands. The failure is visible, not silent, but locating the floor and working around it costs the operator manual effort on every occurrence. | A-15 |
| S-48 | ai-bubble-collapse | Frontier-tier model access becomes economically inviable — pricing, provider exits, or a broader AI-investment contraction — leaving operators with only slower, less capable, open-weight models. When frontier capability disappears, the procedural burden an LLM agent used to absorb lands on the human operator instead. | A-16 |
| S-49 | security-restricted-model-access | Some system architecture environments — air-gapped networks, classified or regulated systems, data-residency-restricted deployments — prohibit outbound access to hosted frontier models entirely for security-policy reasons. Operators inside these environments must accomplish the same cognitive work using only local or approved models, with no path to frontier-tier capability regardless of budget. | A-16 |
| S-50 | org-heresy-risk | An operator is already convinced of residuality's value, but their org's prevailing methodology culture treats upfront stressor/attractor analysis as heretical or waterfall-flavored. Surfacing residuality vocabulary directly risks the operator's standing, so they conceal, dilute, or avoid the method even though they're sold on it. | A-17 |
| S-51 | anti-documentation-culture | Engineers whose ethos rejects in-codebase documentation treat @residue:/@stressor: tags as unwelcome clutter — not from skepticism about residuality's value, but from the same standing/cultural-hostility pressure that makes surfacing residuality vocabulary risky elsewhere in the org. Manual annotation never happens in that environment, so tag-based residue tracking is dead on arrival. | A-17 |
| S-52 | prying-eyes-vengeful-action | An outsider with motive — a political rival, an executive looking to kill the initiative, an auditor — discovers raw residuality artifacts (walks, attractor language, candid failure narratives) and reads them not neutrally but as ammunition. The danger isn't that the reasoning is unfinished; it's that the observer's locked priors turn even sound reasoning into a weapon against the operator. | A-17 |
| S-53 | groupthink-psych-safety | A walk can satisfy nominal headcount (e.g. P-10's stakeholder + direct-user bar) while a hierarchical or blame-driven team culture suppresses genuine dissent — junior voices defer to senior ones, minority concerns carry social cost, candid failure-mode naming gets punished rather than rewarded. Conversely, a psychologically safe team can still lack headcount or role diversity — everyone present shares the same exposure to the system and simply hasn't seen what a different role would surface. Either gap alone produces a walk that feels thorough — attendance met, atmosphere felt open — but isn't: neither condition alone guarantees recorded stressors reflect the real state space. | A-18 |
| S-54 | ai-model-monoculture | AI vendors increasingly train on overlapping public corpora and converge through similar RLHF alignment processes. An operator who assigns different personas to different models, expecting genuine perspective divergence, gets convergent reasoning and risk-posture back anyway — the diversity they believe 'multiple models' bought them is illusory, because the vendors themselves are subject to the same competitive and training pressures that narrowed the field to begin with. | A-18 |
| S-55 | blind-before-synthesis | Group discussion collapses independent perspectives toward whatever position surfaces first or carries the most social weight, before any of it reaches the ledger — the record ends up looking like consensus even when consensus was never actually tested. | A-18 |
| S-56 | adversarial-purpose-validation | A purpose that reads as safely supporting the positive attractor may, under sustained adversarial pressure, turn out to produce the opposite effect. | S-57 | landscape-growth-recall | As the ledger grows past what an operator can hold in working memory, coherent longitudinal grasp of the landscape degrades — the operator records duplicate or contradictory forces, or makes decisions blind to what's already there, because re-reading 40+ stressors before every session isn't viable. | A-19 |
| S-58 | contradictory-tooling-instructions | Residuality has little presence in model pretraining corpora, so an agent's prior on residual's CLI conventions (cwd-relative storage, config-driven paths) is weak. | S-59 | sidecar-branch-monoculture | A single, fixed-name git-sidecar branch stores metadata for every working branch in the repo, so switching feature branches doesn't switch which metadata tip is being read or written. | A-04 |
| S-60 | agent-hook-fragmentation | Agent tooling changes frequently and exposes incompatible, incomplete, or no pre-compaction, post-compaction, and turn lifecycle hooks. | A-20 |

139	## Terminology
140	| term | definition |
141	|---|---|
142	| stressor | a narrative describing how the business system moves to a different attractor without requiring probability or consensus |
143	| attractor | a recurring multivariate condition a system returns to; described by a positive state (what keeps it going) and a negative state (what it looks like when pressure fails) — not classified as solely positive or solely negative |
144	| residue | what is left over after stress or intent is applied; the unit of architectural change; a residue contains either a stressor (negative residual) or a purpose (positive residual) |
145	| walk | iterative traversal of a domain with multiple stakeholders to build rich layered understanding |
146	| criticality | the point at which a system has the right balance of N (nodes) and K (links) to be resilient to unknown stressors without being chaotic |
147	| hyperliminal | describing coupling that is invisible until a stressor activates it — shared stress response across components |
148	| fusion | combining two components that share identical stress-response patterns into one to safely reduce N |
149	| fission | splitting a component with excessive stress surface (high K) into smaller parts to reduce coupling |
150	| trait | a verifiable statement of a desired outcome — end state, mode of operation, or way of being — of the form subject + verb + predicate; must use defined terminology |
151	| persona | a stakeholder voice used during stressor-walk to surface concerns and desires from a specific role's perspective |
152	| naive-architecture | the first-pass architecture produced before stressor analysis; the starting point for residual analysis |
153	| skill | a versioned agent-agnostic prompt document encoding a specific methodology step in the residuality workflow |
154	| residual-architecture | architecture that has considered many stressors and purposes; the post-exposure architecture under evaluation; contrasted with naive-architecture |
155	| resilient-architecture | a residual-architecture that has reached criticality |
156	| operator | human-actor or agent-actor that runs residual commands and skill sessions; may work alone or with additional outside input; contrasted with prospect |
157	| whole-system-residue | a residue whose surviving change may land outside the software boundary — hardware, process, organization, or policy — when that change answers the stressor better than a software-only patch |
158	| negative-residual | a residue whose content is a stressor; the negative side of residual analysis |
159	| positive-residual | a residue whose content is a purpose; the positive side of residual analysis |
160	| outcome | what a trait encodes: a desired end state, mode of operation, journey, or way of being — not limited to one-off completion events |
161	| probability-framing | encoding exploration as likelihoods or risk scores; in non-ergodic hyperliminal systems probabilities are exclusionary opinions — they collapse unseen attractors and block full state-space walks because only pre-weighted futures get attention |
162	| prospect | a potential operator who has not yet adopted residuality; may be evaluating efficacy before becoming an operator |
163	| user | a person or system that uses the application or service being architected; not the residual operator or prospect |
164	| ergodic boundary | The boundary, defined per architecture iteration, between the ergodic core under architectural consideration and the non-ergodic torrent of the hyperliminal; force descriptions primarily beyond it concern architecture, while descriptions within it concern component dynamics. |
165	| component dynamic | Behavior explained within an ergodic boundary by the operation and interaction of known components rather than by a force originating primarily beyond that boundary. |
166	| architecture iteration | A time-bounded candidate arrangement of components and boundaries against which forces, attractors, and residues are interpreted. |
167	| actor | A definable entity whose behavior or properties are relevant to residual analysis. |
168	| meta-stressor | a stressor whose target is the practice of residuality within an organization rather than the project under architecture — concerning management decisions, teammate bias, or other organizational friction against practicing residuality itself |
169	| meta-attractor | a recurring state that meta-stressors push the residuality practice toward or away from, scoped to sustaining the practice itself rather than the project being architected |
170	| meta-purpose | a behavioral contract for a meta-attractor; canonically, practicing residuality theory in a way that helps both the individual operator and the organization |
171	| walk-persona | a persona voice used during stressor-walk to surface project-state concerns from a specific role's perspective, as distinguished from a defense-persona |
172	| defense-persona | a simulated outsider persona voice used to rehearse how residuality artifacts and pitches will land with a specific external audience, as distinguished from a walk-persona |
173	| outsider | an actor outside the residuality practice — audience, gatekeeper, evaluator, or adversary — whose reception of residuality artifacts is simulated or tracked separately from the operator and prospect |
174	| defense-pitch | a practiced communication artifact, refined through defense-strategy brainstorming and defense-progress history, used to advance residuality concerns in team or organizational communication |

178	| agent-actor | An actor backed by digital intelligence. |

189	
190	### attractors
191	
192	**Attractor** — a recurring *system state*, not a mission statement. Describe healthy (`positive_state`) and broken (`negative_state`) sides of the same coin. One attractor per stable behavioral mode; split compound "and" goals into separate attractors.
193

195	
196	**Stressors** — forces that push the system from the positive attractor toward the negative. Coherence matters, not likelihood. Archaeological source: `git log --stat --oneline | head -40` surfaces wide-spanning commits (coupling the architecture was naive to) and recurring churn (rework the design did not anticipate).

199	
200	**Purposes** — behavioral contracts that must hold for the attractor to remain stable. Each purpose is a feature or behavior that, if absent or broken, moves the system toward its negative attractor state.

# Residual Context — tdd-implement

## Verify status
Policy: `super_strict` / validation.strict = **true**

Ledger checks passed. Proceed Socratically with the skill.

## Fluent capture
Metadata (`residual add stressor|purpose|attractor|term|persona`) works in **any order**, at **any phase**, without invoking a skill. Skills are **selectable analytical lenses** — not mandatory gates. `verify all` enforces structure, not ceremony order.

## Attractors
| id | name | positive_state | negative_state |
|---|---|---|---|
| A-01 | Methodology Credibility | The residuality method has demonstrable evidence of efficacy that is communicable to prospects | The residuality method looks like ungrounded ceremony — prospects cannot evaluate its claims empirically |
| A-02 | Terminology Drift | Lexicon aliases cover plural hyphen and phrase forms; outcome validation hits defined terms without false rejects | Outcomes fail validation; lexicon grows stale; operator sessions invent contradictory terms |
| A-03 | Skill Staleness | Installed stubs match embedded skill versions or delegate content to the binary; skill-check stays green | Operators work from outdated methodology; skill-check reports version mismatch |
| A-04 | Data Fragmentation | Forces, residues, sessions, and format migration keep residual/ consistent under concurrent and migrated writes | verify all returns violations; change-detection is ignored; no trustworthy baseline for FMEA or ATAM |
| A-05 | Residuals Incongruence | residual/ mirrors the proposed architecture_set; residues resolve to registry names; tag-scan suggestions align with verification | Obsolete component tokens remain; skill-data surfaces stale or empty metadata; analysis is grounded in fabricated architecture |
| A-06 | Fluent Architecture Capture | Stressors and purposes land mid-session without phase ceremony; a-la-carte skills remain usable; verify enforces structure not order | Operators over-gate phases or abandon the tool as too rigid |
| A-07 | Software-Only Tunnel Vision | Operator examines whole-system-residue before recording a software-only naive change | Stressors are forced into brittle software zags when hardware, process, organization, or policy would survive better |
| A-08 | Tooling Circumvention | operators and agents use residual CLI for all data operations; direct file edits are reserved for operations the tool does not support | operators bypass the CLI with direct CSV edits, scripts, or raw mutations; ID generation, idempotency, and verify are silently skipped |
| A-09 | Agent Framework Coherence | The agent understands the residuality framework and its terms | The agent fails to understand the residuality framework or its terms |
| A-10 | Initialization Completion | The agent initializes the ledger before entering framework steps | The agent jumps into framework steps before initialization is complete |
| A-11 | Naive Change Comprehension | The agent understands naive_change as the mechanistic adjustment made to counter a stressor or support a purpose. | The agent uses naive_change to restate pressure, describe inaction, or predict failure, leaving the force without an architectural response. |
| A-12 | Force Record Semantics | Every force separates environmental pressure, mechanistic adjustment, desired outcome, and unchecked attractor state. | Force fields restate or contradict one another, leaving the architecture response and desired state ambiguous. |
| A-13 | Force Landscape Legibility | Distinct real-world force configurations remain visible even when available evidence aggregates observations or emphasizes common behavior. | Evidence hides or excludes coherent force configurations, shaping the residual-architecture against a narrowed environment. |
| A-14 | Shared Framework Comprehension | Agent and operator retain shared understanding because dialogue uses human-readable names, stable force shortnames, and clearly distinguished field meanings. | Dialogue relies on opaque IDs and implicit schema knowledge, forcing the operator to translate references and losing continuity between sessions. |
| A-15 | Model Capability Variance | Skills produce trustworthy results across the range of model capability an operator actually invokes them with, without the operator having to notice and manually work around degradation. | A skill's output visibly degrades when the invoking model can't meet the task's cognitive demands — obvious, not silent, but costly: the operator spends manual effort locating and compensating for the gap, session by session, that would be better spent elsewhere. |
| A-16 | Powerful Model Availability | A model powerful enough for the task remains available to the operator. | Powerful models become unavailable to the operator, leaving only slower, less-capable, open-weight models, and shifting procedural burden a powerful model used to absorb onto the operator instead. |
| A-17 | Practitioner Standing | Operator can apply and discuss residuality-shaped reasoning inside their org's prevailing methodology culture without professional or political risk. | Surfacing residuality vocabulary reads as heretical or waterfall-flavored to agile-purist colleagues and management — operator conceals or waters down the method even though they're already convinced, muting its benefit. |
| A-18 | Perspective Coverage Fidelity | The operator's set of consulted perspectives — human and/or AI — actually spans divergent viewpoints: sufficient headcount and genuine psychological safety, sufficient model/persona heterogeneity and freedom from training-corpus overlap — so recorded stressors reflect the real state space. | The operator holds a misplaced sense of diverse coverage — nominal thresholds are met (persona count ≥2, multiple models, multiple humans in the room) but groupthink, poor psychological safety, or model/training-corpus overlap collapse the actual diversity achieved. Stressors go undiscovered while the walk feels thorough. |
| A-19 | Operator Landscape Fluency | Operator retains a coherent working model of the force landscape as it scales, recallable without constant reference to the store. | Landscape complexity outpaces the operator's unaided memory — they record duplicate or contradictory forces, or make decisions blind to what's already there, because re-reading dozens of stressors before every session isn't viable. |
| A-20 | Agent hook reliability | Supported agent lifecycle events invoke the right concise guidance once, and unsupported runtimes degrade to installable skills without false claims. | Residual guidance is missed when needed or fires as irrelevant ceremony, so agents learn to ignore it. |

## Stressors
| id | shortname | description | attractor_id |
|---|---|---|---|
| S-01 | skill-version-drift | An operator installs a skill and later updates the binary — the installed skill is now at an older version with different methodology | A-03 |
| S-02 | lexicon-scale-lag | terminology.csv grows to 200+ terms and trait validation becomes prohibitively slow | A-04 |
| S-03 | concurrent-purpose-write | Two operators run purpose-walk concurrently and both append to purposes.csv simultaneously | A-04 |
| S-04 | partial-init-clobber | An operator runs residual init in a directory that already has partial residual/ data — some files exist some don't | A-04 |
| S-05 | skill-token-warn-miss | The token_warn limit is exceeded by a skill and no warning is surfaced | A-03 |
| S-06 | verify-hook-bypass | Terminology validation in the pre-commit hook becomes slow enough that operators bypass it with --no-verify, admitting unverified traits to the repository | A-02 |
| S-07 | skill-stub-burden | The skill install-and-check lifecycle creates ongoing maintenance burden — users must track, update, and reconcile installed stubs that could instead delegate all content to the binary | A-03 |
| S-08 | absent-metadata-session | An operator runs residual skill sessions on a preexisting project with no residual/ metadata — skills assume initialized data and produce empty or misleading outputs rather than pivoting to a capture-first mode | A-05 |
| S-09 | unverified-baseline | A commit lands via --no-verify or direct CSV edit, bypassing the pre-commit hook — residuals data now contains unvalidated state that no skill session can safely trust as a baseline | A-05 |
| S-10 | tag-scan-false-coverage | Third-party libraries, generated files, and non-standard formats resist annotation — operators must manually edit CSVs, making tag-scan coverage readings misleading and creating false integrity signals | A-05 |
| S-11 | cross-store-incongruence | Stressor traits use plural and undefined terminology forms that fail verification, components exist only as free text with no registry, and no cross-store connectivity tests exist — data appears locally valid but fails as a system | A-05 |

| S-16 | proposed-as-actual | An operator interprets residual components as code modules that must be fully implemented, or treats the component list as the actual system rather than a proposed architectural state space — adding five new components for comparison requires the same investment as the baseline, defeating the purpose of exploratory parallel architectures | A-05 |
| S-17 | embedded-component-fields | Stressor and purpose records embed component references directly in their fields — changing a component name or scope requires editing every stressor and purpose that mentions it; the 'which components survive this stressor' analysis has no dedicated home and cannot be versioned, compared, or queried independently | A-04 |
| S-18 | flat-parallel-blind | An operator has accumulated many stressors, purposes, and components across concerns, teams, and parallel architecture sets — the flat matrix/list view with no grouping or subset filter makes relationships invisible and parallel architectures indistinguishable from the baseline; the operator cannot zoom to one attractor, architecture_set, or force cohort without reading the whole grid | A-05 |
| S-19 | purpose-residue-gap | residues.csv as designed in S-17 only carries stressor-sourced rows — purposes have no residue representation, making it impossible to see in one view which purposes are supported or undermined by which component and stressor combinations | A-04 |
| S-20 | silent-residue-clobber | The CLI overwrites residues.csv (and other managed files) without checking for manual modifications — an operator who has annotated residue statuses, added notes, or rearranged rows loses those changes silently; no diff, no warning, no backup; the problem is sharpest for residues.csv but applies to all files | A-05 |
| S-21 | phase-rigidity-assumption | An operator trained on rigid phase-gated methodologies assumes skills must run in order, phases cannot overlap, and metadata must be complete before analysis — the tool does nothing to surface its fluent nature, causing operators to over-structure their workflow or abandon the tool as too prescriptive | A-05 |
| S-22 | prospect-efficacy-doubt | Prospect skepticism of residuality efficacy blocks adoption — without robust studies and empirical alpha/beta perspective measures the method looks like ungrounded ceremony | A-01 |
| S-23 | software-only-zag | Operator prematurely decides on a software fix for a stressor and never examines hardware, process, organization, or policy zig | A-07 |
| S-24 | ceremony-lockout | Operator workflows are not considered — the tool demands a rigid full skill sequence and rejects a-la-carte use, so operators abandon residuality or fake compliance | A-06 |
| S-25 | attractor-valence-blind | Operator cannot tell why a stressor hurts the project because attractors lack paired positive and negative pressure — the stressor has nowhere coherent to land | A-09 |
| S-26 | matrix-viewport-blind | The NKP matrix is hard to read at dogfood scale — coupling heat does not read as a heatmap, row/column totals are missing or easy to lose, and headers/row labels scroll off-screen — so operators miss hyperliminal bands, fission candidates, and which forces drive K | A-06 |
| S-27 | residue-matrix-shape | residues.csv is already matrix-shaped (force × component cells), but at real project scale neither the CLI table nor raw CSV remains usable for filtering, zoom, multi-view exploration, or coherent landscape recall — spreadsheet-friendly shape alone does not yield operator fluency | A-19 |
| S-28 | lexicon-commit-drift | Operators use conventional commit prefixes (fix:/chore:/refactor:) that carry no project vocabulary — git log drifts from lexicon and components.csv | A-02 |
| S-29 | cli-bypass | Agent or operator edits residual/ CSVs directly (Python scripts, raw text edits, sed) for operations the residual CLI already supports — bypassing ID generation, idempotency guards, and verify | A-08 |
| S-30 | persona-context-pollution | When persona voices are generated inline alongside the main conversation they read the same context, share the same mental model, and produce shallow concerns that mirror what the operator already thinks — producing no new information and failing to surface real stressor pressure from external viewpoints | A-05 |
| S-31 | attractor-mission-conflation | An agent prompted to bootstrap an uninitialized ledger conflates an attractor with the system mission statement — bundling multiple concerns and omitting the negative state — producing a ledger that appears populated but carries no bifurcation signal for stressors to push against | A-09 |
| S-32 | force-component-drift | A stressor fires but the components listed on it did not need to change — the force-component mapping was anticipated incorrectly. Over time these mismatches accumulate unchecked: the matrix coupling analysis drifts from empirical reality, and no record exists to identify or correct the pattern | A-05 |
| S-33 | legacy-naive-change-ambiguity | At time of use, the agent encounters existing records and examples that use naive_change for assumptions, untreated behavior, and mechanistic adjustments interchangeably. | A-11 |
| S-34 | component-framed-input | At time of use, an actor supplies an incident or requirement narrative framed entirely through known components, concealing whether any force originates beyond the architecture iteration ergodic boundary. | A-09 |

## Terminology
| term | definition |
|---|---|
| stressor | a narrative describing how the business system moves to a different attractor without requiring probability or consensus |
| attractor | a recurring multivariate condition a system returns to; described by a positive state (what keeps it going) and a negative state (what it looks like when pressure fails) — not classified as solely positive or solely negative |
| residue | what is left over after stress or intent is applied; the unit of architectural change; a residue contains either a stressor (negative residual) or a purpose (positive residual) |
| walk | iterative traversal of a domain with multiple stakeholders to build rich layered understanding |
| criticality | the point at which a system has the right balance of N (nodes) and K (links) to be resilient to unknown stressors without being chaotic |
| hyperliminal | describing coupling that is invisible until a stressor activates it — shared stress response across components |
| fusion | combining two components that share identical stress-response patterns into one to safely reduce N |
| fission | splitting a component with excessive stress surface (high K) into smaller parts to reduce coupling |
| trait | a verifiable statement of a desired outcome — end state, mode of operation, or way of being — of the form subject + verb + predicate; must use defined terminology |
| persona | a stakeholder voice used during stressor-walk to surface concerns and desires from a specific role's perspective |
| naive-architecture | the first-pass architecture produced before stressor analysis; the starting point for residual analysis |
| skill | a versioned agent-agnostic prompt document encoding a specific methodology step in the residuality workflow |
| residual-architecture | architecture that has considered many stressors and purposes; the post-exposure architecture under evaluation; contrasted with naive-architecture |
| resilient-architecture | a residual-architecture that has reached criticality |
| operator | human-actor or agent-actor that runs residual commands and skill sessions; may work alone or with additional outside input; contrasted with prospect |
| whole-system-residue | a residue whose surviving change may land outside the software boundary — hardware, process, organization, or policy — when that change answers the stressor better than a software-only patch |
| negative-residual | a residue whose content is a stressor; the negative side of residual analysis |
| positive-residual | a residue whose content is a purpose; the positive side of residual analysis |
| outcome | what a trait encodes: a desired end state, mode of operation, journey, or way of being — not limited to one-off completion events |
| probability-framing | encoding exploration as likelihoods or risk scores; in non-ergodic hyperliminal systems probabilities are exclusionary opinions — they collapse unseen attractors and block full state-space walks because only pre-weighted futures get attention |
| prospect | a potential operator who has not yet adopted residuality; may be evaluating efficacy before becoming an operator |
| user | a person or system that uses the application or service being architected; not the residual operator or prospect |
| ergodic boundary | The boundary, defined per architecture iteration, between the ergodic core under architectural consideration and the non-ergodic torrent of the hyperliminal; force descriptions primarily beyond it concern architecture, while descriptions within it concern component dynamics. |
| component dynamic | Behavior explained within an ergodic boundary by the operation and interaction of known components rather than by a force originating primarily beyond that boundary. |
| architecture iteration | A time-bounded candidate arrangement of components and boundaries against which forces, attractors, and residues are interpreted. |
| actor | A definable entity whose behavior or properties are relevant to residual analysis. |
| meta-stressor | a stressor whose target is the practice of residuality within an organization rather than the project under architecture — concerning management decisions, teammate bias, or other organizational friction against practicing residuality itself |
| meta-attractor | a recurring state that meta-stressors push the residuality practice toward or away from, scoped to sustaining the practice itself rather than the project being architected |
| meta-purpose | a behavioral contract for a meta-attractor; canonically, practicing residuality theory in a way that helps both the individual operator and the organization |
| walk-persona | a persona voice used during stressor-walk to surface project-state concerns from a specific role's perspective, as distinguished from a defense-persona |
| defense-persona | a simulated outsider persona voice used to rehearse how residuality artifacts and pitches will land with a specific external audience, as distinguished from a walk-persona |
| outsider | an actor outside the residuality practice — audience, gatekeeper, evaluator, or adversary — whose reception of residuality artifacts is simulated or tracked separately from the operator and prospect |
| defense-pitch | a practiced communication artifact, refined through defense-strategy brainstorming and defense-progress history, used to advance residuality concerns in team or organizational communication |
| git-sidecar | an orphan git branch holding the full residual/ metadata tree decoupled from the working branch where code lives |
| stealth-mode | config hosted one directory above the repo root so working-branch commits never touch residual configuration |
| human-actor | An actor backed by human intelligence. |

## Guru

### attractors

**Attractor** — a recurring *system state*, not a mission statement. Describe healthy (`positive_state`) and broken (`negative_state`) sides of the same coin. One attractor per stable behavioral mode; split compound "and" goals into separate attractors.

### stressors

**Stressors** — forces that push the system from the positive attractor toward the negative. Coherence matters, not likelihood. Archaeological source: `git log --stat --oneline | head -40` surfaces wide-spanning commits (coupling the architecture was naive to) and recurring churn (rework the design did not anticipate).

### purposes

**Purposes** — behavioral contracts that must hold for the attractor to remain stable. Each purpose is a feature or behavior that, if absent or broken, moves the system toward its negative attractor state.

### personas

**Personas** — simulation voices for stressor-walk and FMEA. Record at least two distinct personas before deep analysis; verification nudges when fewer exist but capture is not blocked.

### whole-system-residue

Examine **whole-system-residue** (hardware, process, organization, policy zig) before defaulting to a software-only patch. Use `--whole-system --notes` when the surviving change leaves the software boundary.

entries.description:
IMPORTANT: WebFetch WILL FAIL for authenticated or private URLs. Before using this tool, check if the URL points to an authenticated service (e.g. Google Docs, Confluence, Jira, GitHub). If so, look for a specialized MCP tool that provides authenticated access.

- Fetches content from a specified URL and processes it using an AI model
- Takes a URL and a prompt as input
- Fetches the URL content, converts HTML to markdown
- Processes the content with the prompt using a small, fast model
- Returns the model's response about the content
- Use this tool when you need to retrieve and analyze web content

Usage notes:
  - IMPORTANT: If an MCP-provided web fetch tool is available, prefer using that tool instead of this one, as it may have fewer restrictions.
  - The URL must be a fully-formed valid URL
  - HTTP URLs will be automatically upgraded to HTTPS
  - The prompt should describe what information you want to extract from the page
  - This tool is read-only and does not modify any files
  - Results may be summarized if the content is very large
  - Includes a self-cleaning cache (entries expire after 15 minutes) for faster responses when repeatedly accessing the same URL
  - When a URL redirects to a different host, the tool will inform you and provide the redirect URL in a special format. You should then make a new WebFetch request with the redirect URL to fetch the content.
  - For GitHub URLs, prefer using the gh CLI via Bash instead (e.g., gh pr view, gh issue view, gh api).

content.text:
Milestone (a) is complete and independently verified end-to-end:

- **Red → Green**: subagent 1 wrote the moved test suite against stubs (13 genuine `todo!()` panics, not compile errors); subagent 2 implemented `render_matrix`/`render_defense_records`/`render_meta_force_item`/`render_meta_attractor_item`/`render_defense_forms` via Dioxus (`dioxus 0.7.10` + `dioxus-ssr 0.7.10`, purely synchronous, no async runtime pulled in).
- I then did the cutover myself (mechanical, no new logic): renamed `template.html` → `shell.html`, gave `static_export.rs` its own `include_str!`, deleted `html.rs`, repointed `mod.rs`'s `pub use`. Found and removed one piece of dead code the green phase left behind (`esc()` in `matrix.rs`, unused because Dioxus auto-escapes text/attribute interpolation).
- **Independently verified** (not just trusting subagent reports): full suite green (301+4+5+30, 0 failures — the earlier 319 included both old and new copies of the same tests transiently), `residual verify all` passes, `nix develop -c residual view` builds fresh through the flake's crane-based test-gated derivation and produces correct output (matrix table, `data-force-id` attributes, one snapshot script tag). No `unwrap()`/`expect()` outside test code in any new file.
- One documented, non-behavioral divergence: Dioxus never emits bare boolean attributes, so `hidden`/`required`/etc. now render as `hidden="true"` instead of the old bare `hidden` — same effect in browsers, no test depends on the old form.
- `html.rs`/old `template.html` are gone; nothing else in the crate referenced them.

Net diff: 8 files, +1849/−344 (most of that is `Cargo.lock` from the two new deps).

Want me to commit this now (milestone (a) only, following this repo's `<component>: S-<nn>: summary` convention — I'd use `cli: S-27:` continuing the `residue-matrix-shape` lineage, since that's what the earlier matrix work also used), or hold off and continue straight into milestone (b) — the feature-gated `live` skeleton — first?
